title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Combined Deployment, Day‑2 Ops, Packaging, Upgrade & Rollback
author: Aisha Patel
content:
## Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended guidance for private deployments (VPC and on‑prem), including reference architectures, packaging requirements, day‑2 operational practices, upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer requirements library. It is intended for Solutions Engineers, SREs, and Customer Engineering teams executing or supporting private deployments.

Summary: this doc provides a prescriptive, end‑to‑end checklist and runbook to reduce deployment risk, meet SLAs, and standardize customer expectations.

---

## Goals and scope

- Provide a repeatable deployment pattern that supports both cloud VPC‑hosted private control plane and fully on‑prem air‑gapped installs.
- Define packaging, networking, capacity, and security requirements.
- Provide day‑2 operational runbooks for backups, monitoring, scaling, and incident recovery.
- Define safe upgrade and rollback procedures and verification checks.
- Consolidate a customer requirements library for pre‑sales and onboarding.

This doc covers Redwood control plane components and the inference runtime package delivered to the customer environment. It does not replace customer legal/compliance contracts or site‑specific change windows — those are coordinated through the Customer Success team.

---

## Reference architectures (high level)

1) VPC Private Deployment (recommended for regulated cloud customers)

- Topology: Customer VPC with private subnets hosting the inference nodes; Redwood‑managed control plane endpoints exposed via PrivateLink (AWS) / Private Service Connect (GCP) or customer‑hosted control plane in the VPC.
- Components:
  - Inference fleet (GPU nodes) behind an internal load balancer
  - Redis/etcd for KV and ephemeral coordination (optional: customer‑managed or bundled)
  - Object storage (S3‑compatible) for model artifacts and checkpointing (can be customer S3/GCS or local NFS)
  - Metrics & logs forwarding via Fluentd/OTel to customer observability or Redwood's secure collector
- Typical security controls: VPC endpoint policy, security groups locking to CIDR ranges, KMS integration for model keys.
- Sizing guidance: Start with 3 inference servers (NVIDIA A10/A16 or equivalent) for HA, scale based on qps and batch sizing described below.

2) On‑Prem (air‑gapped)

- Topology: Customer data center with isolated network. Redwood provides an on‑prem bundle (container images, operator manifests, packaging tool) and a local control plane instance.
- Components:
  - Kubernetes cluster (preferred) or bare‑metal host pool running packaged runtime
  - Internal artifact registry (Harbor) for images, or offline image install scripts
  - Local object store (minio) or NFS for models
  - HSM/KMS bridge if required for key management
- Constraints: No external outbound traffic by default. Admins must allow curated IPs only for license checks if requested and approved.

3) Hybrid (control plane in Redwood but inference in customer VPC/on‑prem)

- Used when customers require Redwood support & telemetry but want compute in own environment. Encrypted control channel & strict telemetry sampling are configurable.

---

## Packaging and distribution (on‑prem bundle)

Required deliverables for on‑prem package:

- Container images: inference runtime, sidecars (metrics & logs), updater, health‑manager.
- Kubernetes manifests / Helm chart or systemd unit files for bare metal.
- Offline installation script (tar.gz) including images, manifests, and step‑by‑step installer.
- SHA256 checksums & signed manifests.
- Packaging metadata file (packaging-version, compatible-k8s-versions, required-node-roles).
- Configuration templates: config.yaml with placeholder secrets, networking variables, storage endpoints.
- Upgrade bundle with migration scripts and rollback artifacts.

Packaging checklist (pre‑release to customer):

- [ ] Images built from pinned commit + reproducible build notes.
- [ ] All images signed and checksums included.
- [ ] Helm chart linted and chart.schema.json validated.
- [ ] Compatibility matrix included for CUDA/cuDNN/driver versions.
- [ ] Operator docs and CLI binary for offline operations provided.

Minimum supported environment (example):

| Component | Minimum | Recommended | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Kubernetes | 1.24 | 1.26 | CRD‑based operator requires RBAC |
| GPU drivers | NVIDIA driver 525.x | driver 535.x | Match runtime CUDA compatibility |
| GPUs | 1x A10 | 4x A10 | Single-node allowed for dev only |
| Disk | 500GB | 2TB NVMe | Model cache & logs |
| RAM | 32GB | 256GB | Depends on concurrency |

Note: Represent disks as mount points with fsync guarantees for checkpoint integrity.

---

## Network & security requirements

Network controls (VPC):

- Private subnets for inference nodes; public subnets unnecessary.
- Internal LB with health check path /_healthz.
- Security groups: allow inbound from customer app subnet and control plane CIDRs.
- Egress allowed only to customer S3/GCS endpoints and Redwood PrivateLink endpoints (when hybrid).

Security controls (on‑prem):

- Image registry access limited to operator account.
- TLS termination either at LB (customer) or in‑pod sidecar.
- Secrets stored in KMS/HSM; if not available, use sealed secrets pattern with operator.
- Audit logging: all admin actions must be forwarded to customer SIEM (syslog/OTLP).

Compliance checklist:

- [ ] KMS keys provisioned and policies reviewed.
- [ ] Network segmentation validated by customer security team.
- [ ] RBAC roles and least privilege verified.
- [ ] Data flow diagram (DFD) provided and signed off.

---

## Day‑2 operations (runbook summaries)

Operational ownership: Customer runs day‑2 ops for on‑prem and VPC compute; Redwood provides runbooks and can optionally operate via managed or co‑managed agreements.

Daily checks (automated recommended):

- Cluster node health: node CPU, GPU utilization, disk pressure. Thresholds: GPU utilization > 90% sustained for 5m => scale up.
- Inference latency P50/P95/P99 compared to baseline. Alert if P95 increased by >25% vs baseline for 10 minutes.
- Error rates (5xx) > 1% of requests => page engineering oncall.
- Model cache hit ratio; if cache miss rate > 30% evaluate cache capacity.

Weekly tasks:

- Model artifact integrity sweep (verify checksums of models loaded).
- Storage cleanup (old checkpoints) per retention policy.
- Test restore from backup (monthly for critical customers).

Incident triage flow (short):

1. Detect: Alert routes to SRE oncall via PagerDuty.
2. Triage: SRE retrieves recent logs via fluentd/OTel, checks /_healthz endpoints.
3. Mitigate: Route traffic to fallback model variant or capacity tier (see rollback).
4. Resolve: If code or config change caused incident, initiate rollback per procedure below.
5. Post‑mortem: Owner updates incident review within 72 hours.

Operational tools and dashboards:

- Required metrics: token throughput, tokens/sec, latency-percentiles, model-load time, GPU mem usage, disk io, pod restarts.
- Recommended dashboards: per‑cluster and per‑model; include action buttons for scaling and model variant swap.

Backups & restores:

- Models and checkpoints: backup frequency depends on model training cadence; default daily snapshot of model registry metadata and weekly snapshot of large model files.
- Store backups in an immutable object store with lifecycle policy.
- Restore verification: after restore, run a smoke test suite of 10 canonical prompts and compare embeddings/checksums.

---

## Upgrade procedure (major/minor)

Scope: Applies to runtime binary, operator/helm chart, and model catalog changes.

Preflight checks (to run 24‑72h before window):

- [ ] Validate packaging checksums and signatures.
- [ ] Confirm compatibility matrix (OS, drivers, k8s).
- [ ] Run upgrade dry‑run in staging that mirrors production traffic.
- [ ] Communicate change window to customer stakeholders and schedule maintenance page if required.

Step‑by‑step (controlled rolling upgrade):

1. Snapshot current state: record running versions, active model list, and production traffic baseline.
2. Scale up capacity by +20% (if capacity allows) to preserve headroom.
3. Upgrade non‑critical control‑plane components first (metrics collector, sidecars). Validate logs & metrics.
4. Use canary strategy: upgrade 1 node or 5% of capacity, route 1‑2% of traffic. Run acceptance tests (latency, correctness).
5. If canary looks good for 15‑30 minutes, proceed with incremental batches (10‑20% every 10‑15 minutes).
6. After all nodes upgraded, run full smoke tests (end‑to‑end generation tests and stress tests).
7. Reconcile any configuration drift and remove temporary scaling.
8. Publish upgrade notes and update packaging version.

Upgrade verification checklist:

- [ ] Health endpoints green across all nodes.
- [ ] Latency P95 within +10% of baseline.
- [ ] Error rate <= previous window.
- [ ] Model outputs within established tolerance (see eval harness).

Abort criteria (immediate rollback triggers):

- P95 latency > 2x baseline for more than 10 minutes.
- Error rate > 5% or sustained increase > 2x normal for 5 minutes.
- Canary fails correctness or QA smoke tests.

---

## Rollback procedure (safe rollback)

Principles: always have a tested rollback path; make incremental, reversible changes; ensure stateful components' compatibility.

Preconditions: rollback artifacts must be bundled with upgrade (previous images, helm rollback manifests, DB migration rollback scripts).

Rollback steps (fast path):

1. Immediately stop sending new deployments to the upgraded nodes (remove from LB).
2. If running on k8s: helm rollback to previous release revision for the operator/chart. If containerized: redeploy previous image tag.
3. For stateful migrations: run rollback migration scripts in sequence to avoid schema drift.
4. Validate health and smoke tests.
4. Reintroduce nodes to LB gradually once healthy.

Post‑rollback analysis:

- Record precise failure mode and timeline.
- Recreate failure in staging and produce a remediation plan.
- Update packaging and upgrade checklist to prevent recurrence.

---

## Customer requirements library (pre‑sales & onboarding checklist)

Purpose: standardized list of information to collect during scoping calls for private deployments. Use this as a template in the onboarding ticket.

Must‑have (obtain before scheduling deployment):

- Primary contact (Name, role, email, phone) and escalation contact.
- Target deployment mode: VPC / On‑prem / Hybrid.
- Expected QPS and latency SLOs (P95 target).
- Expected concurrency and model catalog (list of models & sizes).
- Cloud provider & region (if VPC).
- Kubernetes version and cluster topology (if on‑prem).
- Available GPUs (model, count) and driver versions.
- Storage endpoints (S3/GCS bucket names or NFS endpoints) and retention policy.
- Network egress policy: allowed outbound CIDRs / proxy requirements.
- KMS/HSM provider details and key policies.
- Compliance/regulatory constraints (SOC2, HIPAA, GDPR) and required evidence.

Nice‑to‑have (accelerates onboarding):

- Logs & metrics endpoint information (SIEM URL, OTLP endpoints).
- Test data and canonical prompt sets for eval.
- Maintenance windows and preferred SLA escalation path.

Template checklist for onboarding ticket (example):

1. Confirm primary contact & security liaison.
2. Capture environment inventory (K8s, nodes, GPUs, network).
3. Validate storage & KMS access.
4. Confirm access method (VPN, direct connect, ExpressRoute, break‑glass SSH).
5. Schedule installation window and preflight review.

## Roles & responsibilities

- Customer: provide infrastructure, networking changes, KMS/HSM, and day‑2 ops (unless co‑managed).
- Redwood Solutions Engineering: packaging delivery, installation guidance, operator training.
- Redwood SRE / Private Deployments team: verify health during handoff, support first 30 days of incidents, assist with upgrades during co‑managed engagements.
- Customer Success: coordinate timelines, training, and runbooks handover.

## Troubleshooting quick reference

Common failure modes and first checks:

- Nodes failing to start: check driver/kernel compatibility and /var/log/redwood/installer.log.
- High latency after deployment: check batch configuration, model quantization mismatch, and KV cache warmup.
- Models failing to load: verify model checksum and storage permissions (403 errors).
- Image pull failures: ensure registry credentials or offline image installation applied.

Useful CLI snippets:

- Check health: curl -s https://<internal-lb>/_healthz | jq
- List pods (k8s): kubectl get pods -n redwood --show-labels
- Force rollback (helm): helm rollback redwood-runtime <revision> --namespace redwood

---

## Appendix: smoke tests and acceptance criteria

Acceptance test suite (run post‑upgrade / post‑deploy):

1. Connectivity: 10x rapid connect / disconnect cycles to ensure no connection leaks.
2. Latency smoke: run 100 requests against production prompt set; P95 < target + 10%.
3. Correctness: for 10 canonical prompts, outputs must match baseline evaluation signatures.
4. Load test: ramp to 125% expected qps for 5 minutes to ensure graceful degradation.

Artifacts to store with release:
- pack-metadata.yaml
- pre-upgrade-state.json (versions & active models)
- smoke-test-results.json
